title: Geography · Non-exam content (Terms 1–2, 4)
exam_focus: Content outside this coastal unit exam: human wellbeing and development indicators (GDP/HDI), population structure, circle sentencing and ACCOs, geographical skills (ternary graphs, area and grid references), and climate change (FLICC, enhanced greenhouse effect, coral bleaching, ocean acidification, sea level rise case studies).

questions.stem: Why do geographers use GDP per capita rather than total GDP when comparing the wellbeing of different countries?
options: It divides GDP by population, so countries of different sizes can be compared
It measures only the income earned by the very richest people in that country
It removes the need for any other development measure or index
It measures the value of unpaid work done inside the household
questions.explanation_en: GDP per capita is GDP divided by population, which removes the problem that large countries naturally have large totals. It still does not show how evenly income is distributed, though, and it cannot replace an indicator such as HDI.
questions.source: Term 1 · Week 2 Global — Measuring and Mapping Human Wellbeing

questions.stem: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines which three dimensions?
options: Health, education and standard of living (GNI per capita)
Population size, land area and length of coastline
GDP, inflation rate and the unemployment rate
Life expectancy, birth rate and the death rate
questions.explanation_en: The three HDI dimensions are health, education and standard of living. Because it measures health and education as well as income, the HDI is more comprehensive than a single economic indicator such as GDP.
questions.source: Term 1 · Week 2 Global — Lesson 3: quantitative (GDP) vs qualitative (HDI)

questions.stem: In the population-pyramid lesson students study China's ageing population. The source states that by 2100, 37.8% of China's population is projected to be aged over 60. Which is the most likely implication of this figure?
options: A smaller workforce supporting a larger elderly group, straining pensions
A rapidly growing labour force that will raise industrial output sharply
A rising birth rate that will require many new schools and many more teachers
A population pyramid with a very wide base and a much narrower top
questions.explanation_en: An elderly population of nearly 40% means a higher dependency ratio, a smaller workforce and financial pressure on health care and aged care. A 'population pyramid with a very wide base and a much narrower top', by contrast, describes a high birth rate and an expanding population — the opposite of an ageing one.
questions.source: Term 1 · Weeks 3–4 Geographic Skills — China's Ageing Population (37.8% over 60 by 2100)

questions.stem: Describe the spatial pattern of advantage and disadvantage in Sydney and explain one factor that produces it.
questions.answer: Advantage is concentrated in the east, north and harbour-side suburbs, while disadvantage is concentrated in the west and south-west. Higher incomes, employment and better access to services, schools and healthy food cluster in the advantaged areas, while high housing costs push lower-income households further from those opportunities.
questions.explanation_en: The answer needs 'pattern plus one cause'. The pattern is the contrast between the east and north on one side and the west and south-west on the other; the cause can be income, housing prices, or access to services and employment, following the course scaffold.
questions.source: Term 1 · Weeks 7–8 Local — Sydney's socio-economic divide (East vs West)

criteria.t: Describes the pattern of advantage: it is concentrated in the east, north and harbour-side suburbs
Describes the pattern of disadvantage: it is concentrated in the west and south-west
Explains one factor producing the pattern, such as high housing costs pushing lower-income households away from areas where income, employment and access to services cluster

questions.stem: Circle sentencing in NSW is best described as:
options: A sentencing process where Elders sit with a magistrate after a guilty verdict
A police caution given before any charge is laid against an offender
A process that replaces the court entirely with a community tribunal
A separate court that hears only cases involving young offenders
questions.explanation_en: Circle sentencing happens after a guilty verdict: community members and Elders take part in deciding the sentence, which improves cultural appropriateness and reduces reoffending. It does not replace the court, and it is not a pre-trial process.
questions.source: Term 2 · Week 2.3 First Nations Justice — Action (circle sentencing)

questions.stem: On a ternary graph, what do the three axes represent?
options: Three parts of a whole that add to 100%, read off one point
Three separate graphs placed side by side on one page
Three separate time periods shown along a single horizontal line
Three countries compared by their total population
questions.explanation_en: A ternary graph shows the proportions of three components that add to 100%, such as employment structure or soil composition. Each axis gives one component, and the three values must add to 100%.

questions.topic: Geographical skills · Area and grid references
questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an area reference (AR) from a grid reference (GR)?
options: An AR uses four figures for a square; a GR uses six for a point
An AR uses six figures for a point; a GR uses four for a grid square
An AR gives elevation in metres; a GR gives distance in km
An AR is used on small-scale maps; a GR only on précis maps
questions.explanation_en: An AR uses four digits to locate a square of about 1 km × 1 km, while a GR uses six digits to locate a specific point inside that square, accurate to 100 m. Do not mix up the order of the digits.
questions.source: Term 1 · Weeks 3–4 Topographic Skills — AR, GR and elevation

questions.stem: Explain one way circle sentencing could improve outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples compared with a standard court process.
questions.answer: It involves Elders and community members in deciding the sentence, so the outcome reflects the offender's community and culture and the offender is held accountable in front of people they know. This can increase respect for the process and reduce reoffending, which matters given the over-representation of Aboriginal people in custody.
questions.explanation_en: You need 'mechanism → result': community and Elder involvement produces cultural safety and accountability, which makes the sentence more likely to be accepted and reduces reoffending. Writing only 'fairer' gains no marks.
questions.source: Term 2 · Weeks 2.3 / 3.1 First Nations Justice — Action & Outcome

criteria.t: Explains the mechanism: circle sentencing involves Elders and community members in deciding the sentence

Explains the outcome: the sentence reflects the offender's community and culture and they are held accountable before people they know, which can increase respect for the process and reduce reoffending
Links this to the over-representation of Aboriginal people in custody, explaining why improved outcomes matter

questions.stem: In the climate misinformation lessons, 'cherry-picking' as a science-denial technique means:
options: Selecting data that support a position while ignoring contrary data
Choosing only the most reliable long-term dataset available
Repeating an experiment until the results agree with the theory you hold
Refusing to accept any scientific evidence whatsoever on the topic
questions.explanation_en: Cherry-picking is one of the five FLICC techniques: only the data points that support the position are selected and the overall trend is ignored. The reflection questions in class are designed to make you notice this.

questions.stem: How does the enhanced greenhouse effect differ from the natural greenhouse effect?
options: Human greenhouse gas emissions trap more infrared radiation, adding to warming
Human activity has removed the natural effect, so less heat is trapped
The natural effect involves only incoming solar radiation, with no re-emission of heat
The enhanced effect is caused by more solar radiation reaching Earth
questions.explanation_en: The natural greenhouse effect makes the Earth habitable; the extra greenhouse gases released by human activity strengthen it, so more infrared radiation is absorbed and re-radiated back to the surface. Telling the two apart is a common exam point.
questions.source: Term 4 · Lesson 2.2 What are the causes of climate change? (Part 1)

questions.stem: How does rising sea temperature cause coral bleaching?
options: Heat stress makes corals expel their symbiotic algae, losing colour and food
Warmer water dissolves the corals' calcium carbonate skeleton directly
Corals absorb more dissolved carbon dioxide and so grow much faster
Warmer water multiplies the algae living inside corals, making them overgrow faster
questions.explanation_en: Corals live in a symbiotic relationship with zooxanthellae. When heat stresses them, the corals expel the zooxanthellae and lose both their colour and their main food source; if the heat persists, the coral dies rather than simply turning white.
questions.source: Term 4 · Lesson 3.3 How does sea temperature rise lead to coral bleaching?

questions.topic: Climate change · Global warming vs climate change
questions.stem: Lesson 2.1 asks students to distinguish between global warming and climate change. Which statement is correct?
options: Global warming is the rise in average temperature; climate change also covers rainfall and sea level
Global warming refers only to sea temperatures; climate change only to air temperatures
The two terms mean exactly the same thing and can be used interchangeably in every case
Climate change happens naturally, while global warming is a separate process unrelated to it
questions.explanation_en: Global warming is the rise in average temperature, which is only one part of climate change — a broader concept that also includes changes in precipitation, sea level, ice caps and extreme weather events.
questions.source: Term 4 · Lesson 2.1 EVIDENCE — distinguishing global warming from climate change

questions.stem: Explain how ocean acidification impacts marine life.
questions.answer: The ocean absorbs extra carbon dioxide, which forms carbonic acid and lowers the pH of seawater. This reduces the availability of carbonate ions, so organisms such as corals, shellfish and some plankton cannot build or maintain their shells and skeletons, which then affects the wider food chain.
questions.explanation_en: The mechanism involves: CO₂ dissolving in seawater → forming carbonic acid → decreasing pH → reducing carbonate ions → making it difficult for calcifying organisms to form shells and skeletons → affecting the food chain.
questions.source: Term 4 · Lesson 4.1 Ocean Acidification & Its Impact on Marine Life

criteria.t: Explains that the ocean absorbs extra carbon dioxide, which forms carbonic acid and lowers the pH of seawater
Explains that fewer carbonate ions are available, so corals, shellfish and some plankton cannot build or maintain their shells and skeletons
Explains that this then affects the wider food chain

questions.topic: Climate change · Sea level rise examples
questions.stem: Using the Solomon Islands case study, explain two impacts of sea level rise on low-lying Pacific nations.
questions.answer: First, higher seas and larger storm surges erode beaches and inundate low-lying land, so villages, gardens and fresh-water supplies are lost and communities are forced to relocate. Second, salt water intrudes into soil and groundwater, reducing the land available for growing food and increasing dependence on outside aid.
questions.explanation_en: This can be answered on two levels: environmental and land (erosion, flooding, saltwater intrusion) and socio-economic (forced relocation, food and water shortages, reliance on aid).
questions.source: Term 4 · Lesson 3.2 Sea level rise — Solomon Islands case study

criteria.t: Explains that higher seas and larger storm surges erode beaches and inundate low-lying land
Explains the social consequence: villages, gardens and fresh-water supplies are lost and communities are forced to relocate
Explains that salt water intrudes into soil and groundwater, reducing land for growing food and increasing dependence on outside aid
